lessons.titleEnglish: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objectiveEnglish: Say what you have, need and want at breakfast, and ask what the café has.
lessons.titleFrenchCourseEnglish: Avoir, Il y a and Needs at the Café
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Say what you have, need and want at a café, and ask whether the café has something.
lessons.focusEnglish: Have and need with avoir, il y a and avoir besoin de; polite requests with je voudrais; il faut for rules such as paying at the register; du/de la/des for amounts.
lessons.focusFrench: Avoir (j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont) ; il y a ; avoir besoin de ; je voudrais ; il faut + infinitif ; du/de la/des.

words.noteEnglish: Jus alone means juice of any kind. Pressé means freshly squeezed and is common in French cafés.
Pain grillé is toast. In Québec, you will also hear des rôties.
Pronounced BUHR. Butter is always le beurre.
Confiture is the everyday word for jam or preserves in France.
Use les fruits for fruit in general or several pieces of fruit.
Pronounced TAY. The accent on é is part of the spelling.
A paper napkin in a café is often called une serviette en papier.
Pronounced kwee-YEHR. A small spoon for coffee is une petite cuillère.
The word has the ending -ette, which is feminine.

words.en: Do you have fresh orange juice?
words.fr: Vous avez du jus d'orange pressé ?
words.noteEnglish: Pressé means freshly squeezed; frais can mean fresh or chilled. Vous avez is a polite question with a server.

words.fr: Il y a du pain grillé ?
words.noteEnglish: Il y a means there is or there are, and it never changes form.

words.fr: J'ai besoin d'une serviette, s'il vous plaît.
words.noteEnglish: Avoir besoin de + noun means need. Before a vowel, de becomes d', as in d'une.

words.en: I'd like a tea without sugar.
words.fr: Je voudrais un thé sans sucre.
words.noteEnglish: Je voudrais (I would like) is the polite way to order. Sans means without.

words.en: Do you have to pay at the register?
words.fr: Il faut payer à la caisse ?
words.noteEnglish: Il faut + infinitive means one must or you have to. Payer is the verb to pay.
French uses avoir faim (to have hunger), not être. Use très (very), not beaucoup, before faim.

lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Tell the server you are very hungry, ask if they have fresh orange juice, then say you need a fork and a napkin, please.
lessons.speakingFrench: J'ai très faim. Vous avez du jus d'orange pressé ? J'ai besoin d'une fourchette et d'une serviette, s'il vous plaît.

english: In a café in Oaxaca, Emma tells the server Luis: I'm very hungry.
Emma: Do you have fresh orange juice?
Luis: Yes, and there is also fresh fruit with breakfast.
Emma: Is there toast?
Luis: Yes, the toast comes with butter and jam.
Emma: I'd like a tea without sugar and a spoon, please.
Emma: I also need a fork and a napkin, please.
Luis: Sure, and you have to pay at the register at the end.
french: Dans un café à Lyon, Emma dit au serveur Luis : J'ai très faim.
Emma : Vous avez du jus d'orange pressé ?
Luis : Oui, et il y a aussi des fruits frais au petit-déjeuner.
Emma : Il y a du pain grillé ?
Luis : Oui, le pain grillé est servi avec du beurre et de la confiture.
Emma : Je voudrais un thé sans sucre et une cuillère, s'il vous plaît.
Emma : J'ai aussi besoin d'une fourchette et d'une serviette, s'il vous plaît.
Luis : Bien sûr, et il faut payer à la caisse à la fin.
englishFrenchCourse: In a café in Lyon, Emma tells the server Luis: I'm very hungry.
Emma: Do you have fresh orange juice?
Luis: Yes, and there is also fresh fruit with breakfast.
Emma: Is there toast?
Luis: Yes, the toast comes with butter and jam.
Emma: I'd like a tea without sugar and a spoon, please.
Emma: I also need a fork and a napkin, please.
Luis: Sure, and you have to pay at the register at the end.

teachingNotesEnglish: Avoir means to have: j'ai, tu as, il or elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils or elles ont. Use it for hunger and needs: j'ai faim, j'ai besoin de.
Il y a means there is or there are. It never changes, so use it for both one item and several: Il y a du pain grillé ? Il y a des fruits.
Avoir besoin de + noun means to need. De + une becomes d'une before the vowel: j'ai besoin d'une serviette.
Avoir envie de means to feel like or want to: J'ai envie de manger (with a verb), or J'ai envie d'un thé (with a noun). This is an optional extension.
Je voudrais (I would like) is softer and more polite than je veux (I want). Use it to order at a café.
Il faut + infinitive means one must or you have to. Use it for rules, such as paying at the register.
In this fictional Lyon café, Emma asks about fresh orange juice and fruit. Check the actual menu and service rules at each café.
Use vous with a server or any adult you have just met. Move to tu if the other person suggests it or begins using it.
authoringNotesEnglish: The English title, objective, and reading lines are kept exactly as the source gives them. The French-course fields are the learner-facing display text.
Oaxaca and Mexico remain the setting because the English reading lines name them. No prices appear in this lesson, so no euro or peso conversion is needed.
Native French review is still open. The phrase Il faut payer à la caisse is used for the English 'Do you have to pay' line; a native speaker should confirm that it sounds natural in a café.
Le toast is a common alternative to pain grillé in French cafés. This draft uses pain grillé as the standard form.
A France or Québec café variant with local currency is still needed before the lesson claims general French-speaking coverage.

lessons.objectiveEnglish: Say where you are going for breakfast, what you will order, and what you can do at a café.
lessons.titleFrenchCourseEnglish: Going, Doing and Asking Permission at a Café
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Say where you are going and what you plan to order, and ask politely what you can do at a café.
lessons.focusEnglish: Going somewhere and planning with aller and aller + infinitive, doing with faire, and asking permission with pouvoir and est-ce que.
lessons.focusFrench: Aller (je vais, tu vas, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont) + à + lieu ; aller + infinitif pour un projet ; faire (je fais, vous faites) ; pouvoir (je peux, vous pouvez) pour demander la permission ; est-ce que pour une question.

words.noteEnglish: A bakery sells bread and pastries. Un boulanger is the baker.
The café as a place uses the same word as coffee. Un café alone usually means an espresso in France.
Un marché is an open-air market, often held on certain days of the week.
Le comptoir is the bar or counter where you order or sit on a stool.
En terrasse means seated outside at café tables.
La caisse is the till or cash desk where you pay. The person there is le caissier or la caissière.
Les toilettes is the everyday word; les WC is also common on signs.
In France say à emporter; in Québec pour emporter is usual.
Sur place means eaten on the premises, in the café.
À + la stays à la (à la boulangerie). À + le contracts to au (au marché); de + le contracts to du (près du marché).

words.en: I'm going to order the chilaquiles.
words.noteEnglish: Aller + infinitive means going to do something. Commander means to order.
words.enFrenchCourse: I'm going to order the omelette.

words.en: We're going to have breakfast here.
words.fr: Nous allons prendre le petit-déjeuner ici.
words.noteEnglish: Nous allons is the nous form of aller. In everyday speech, on va is also common.

words.en: Can I sit on the terrace?
words.fr: Est-ce que je peux m'asseoir en terrasse ?
words.noteEnglish: En terrasse is the usual café idiom for sitting outdoors. Est-ce que je peux...? asks permission.

words.fr: Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
words.noteEnglish: Par carte means by card. Est-ce que turns a statement into a question.

words.en: Do you make eggs to order?
words.fr: Je peux choisir la cuisson des œufs ?
words.noteEnglish: A natural way to ask whether you may choose how the eggs are cooked; cuisson means cooking method.

lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Tell the barista you will eat here, ask if you can sit on the terrace, and ask if you can pay by card.
lessons.speakingFrench: Je vais manger sur place. Est-ce que je peux m'asseoir en terrasse ? Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?

english: Emma is going to have breakfast at a café near the market.
At the counter, Diego the barista makes coffee.
Emma: I'm going to order the chilaquiles.
Emma: It's for here, not to go.
Emma: Can I sit on the terrace?
Diego: Yes, you can, and the restroom is in the back.
Emma: Can I pay by card?
Diego: Yes, you can pay at the register.
Afterward, Emma is going to go to the bakery for bread.
french: Emma va prendre le petit-déjeuner dans un café près du marché.
Au comptoir, le barista Diego prépare le café.
Emma : Je vais commander l'omelette.
Emma : C'est sur place, pas à emporter.
Emma : Est-ce que je peux m'asseoir en terrasse ?
Diego : Oui, bien sûr, et les toilettes sont au fond.
Emma : Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
Diego : Oui, vous pouvez payer à la caisse.
Ensuite, Emma va aller à la boulangerie chercher du pain.
englishFrenchCourse: Emma is going to have breakfast at a café near the market.
At the counter, Diego the barista makes coffee.
Emma: I'm going to order the omelette.
Emma: It's for here, not to go.
Emma: Can I sit on the terrace?
Diego: Yes, you can, and the restroom is in the back.
Emma: Can I pay by card?
Diego: Yes, you can pay at the register.
Afterward, Emma is going to go to the bakery for bread.

teachingNotesEnglish: Aller means to go: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. Use aller + à + place to say where you are going. À + le becomes au; de + le becomes du. À la stays à la.
Aller + infinitive means going to do something: Je vais commander. It is the usual way to talk about plans in French.
Faire means to make or to do: je fais, nous faisons, vous faites. It is used for making a meal or doing an activity.
Pouvoir means to be able to or can: je peux, tu peux, vous pouvez. Use Est-ce que je peux... ? to ask permission.
Est-ce que puts a question in front of any statement, so you do not have to change the word order.
Ask Où sont les toilettes ? in a café. In Québec, la salle de bain is also common for the restroom; in France it usually means a room with a bath or shower.
France: sur place / à emporter. Québec: pour ici / pour emporter is common.
authoringNotesEnglish: Oaxaca and chilaquiles remain the setting because the English reading lines name them. Chilaquiles stays as a loan word in French.
The eggs-to-order phrase replaces the earlier à la demande wording, which only means on request; native French naturalness review remains open.
The source reading says is going to go. French va aller à la boulangerie preserves the near-future form and is standard French.
No prices or currency conversions appear in this lesson. The French café context is not yet adapted to a France or Québec setting.

lessons.objectiveEnglish: Talk about what you eat and drink for breakfast using present-tense verbs.
lessons.titleFrenchCourseEnglish: Present Tense: What You Eat, Drink and Ask
lessons.objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Talk about what you eat and drink for breakfast, what your family drinks, and where you live, using the French present tense.
lessons.focusEnglish: Present tense of -er verbs (manger, habiter) and useful irregular breakfast verbs (prendre, boire, ouvrir), with vous for adults just met.
lessons.focusFrench: Présent des verbes en -er (manger, habiter) et des verbes courants prendre, boire, ouvrir ; vous avec le personnel et les adultes que l'on vient de rencontrer.

words.noteEnglish: Pain perdu is bread soaked in egg and milk, then cooked; hotel menus vary.
Œufs brouillés are scrambled eggs in France and Québec.
Œufs au plat are fried eggs, usually served with a runny yolk.
Use les fruits for fruit in general or several pieces of fruit.
Fromage is used for all cheese, and it is masculine.
Jambon means ham. Jambon blanc is cooked ham; jambon cru is cured ham.
Le bacon is common in French cafés. Lardons are small cubes of bacon used in cooking.
A fruit salad is une salade de fruits; ask about actual ingredients if you need them confirmed.
Avocat is also the word for lawyer. In a café, it means avocado.
Le porridge is common in France; in Québec, gruau is common. Flocons d'avoine means oat flakes.

words.en: I have breakfast at 8 every day.
words.fr: Je prends le petit-déjeuner à 8 heures tous les jours.
words.noteEnglish: Prendre is irregular: je prends, tu prends, vous prenez. Tous les jours means every day.

words.en: Do you drink coffee or tea?
words.fr: Vous buvez du café ou du thé ?
words.noteEnglish: Boire is irregular: je bois, vous buvez, ils boivent. Vous is the safe form with an adult you have just met.
Habiter is a regular -er verb. Vous is the polite form for someone you have just met.

words.fr: Nous mangeons des œufs et des fruits.
words.noteEnglish: Manger is regular, but the nous form adds an e: nous mangeons.
Mes enfants is the neutral way to say my children. Ils boivent is the ils form of boire.
Ouvrir ends in -ir but takes endings like an -er verb in the present: j'ouvre, vous ouvrez.

lessons.speakingInstructionEnglish: Chat with a fellow guest: say what you eat, ask if they drink coffee or tea, and ask if they live here.
lessons.speakingFrench: Je mange des œufs au petit-déjeuner. Vous buvez du café ou du thé ? Vous habitez ici ?

passage.titleFrench: Au petit-déjeuner de l'hôtel à Lyon
english: Emma has chilaquiles with green salsa for breakfast at her hotel.
Emma: I have breakfast at 8 every day.
Emma puts cheese and avocado on her chilaquiles.
Lucía, another hotel guest, eats scrambled eggs with ham.
Emma: Do you drink coffee or tea?
Lucía: I drink coffee, and my kids eat oatmeal.
Emma: Do you live here in Oaxaca?
Lucía: No, I live in Puebla, and there we eat beans.
Lucía: At home, my husband eats fried eggs with bacon.
french: Emma prend du pain perdu et de la salade de fruits au petit-déjeuner à son hôtel de Lyon.
Emma : Je prends le petit-déjeuner à 8 heures tous les jours.
Emma mange aussi du fromage et de l’avocat sur du pain.
Lucie, une autre cliente de l’hôtel, mange des œufs brouillés avec du jambon.
Emma : Vous buvez du café ou du thé ?
Lucie : Je bois du café, et mes enfants mangent du porridge.
Emma : Vous habitez ici, à Lyon ?
Lucie : Non, j’habite à Grenoble ; chez nous, nous mangeons des œufs et des fruits.
Lucie : À la maison, mon mari mange des œufs au plat avec du bacon.
englishFrenchCourse: Emma has French toast and fruit salad for breakfast at her hotel in Lyon.
Emma: I have breakfast at 8 every day.
Emma also has cheese and avocado on bread.
Lucie, another hotel guest, eats scrambled eggs with ham.
Emma: Do you drink coffee or tea?
Lucie: I drink coffee, and my kids eat oatmeal.
Emma: Do you live here in Lyon?
Lucie: No, I live in Grenoble; at home we eat eggs and fruit.
Lucie: At home, my husband eats fried eggs with bacon.

teachingNotesEnglish: Regular -er verbs drop -er and add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent: je mange, tu manges, il mange, nous mangeons, vous mangez, ils mangent. The -ent ending is silent.
Prendre (to take) is common for breakfast and drinks: je prends le petit-déjeuner, vous prenez un café.
Boire (to drink) is irregular: je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons, vous buvez, ils boivent.
Ouvrir (to open) follows a similar pattern to -er verbs in the present: j'ouvre, tu ouvres, vous ouvrez.
Use vous with adults you have just met and with staff. Switch to tu if the other person suggests it: On peut se tutoyer ? With a friend, Tu bois du café ? is natural.
Les fruits means fruit. In this fictional Lyon hotel scene, Lucie describes her own family breakfast; it is not a regional custom.
authoringNotesEnglish: The source English lines are preserved exactly. French uses vous between Emma and Lucía because they are adult hotel guests who have just met.
Lucía is a guest from Puebla in the Oaxaca frame. The Puebla and Oaxaca references are kept for the English anchors, and no euro conversion is applied.
Porridge stands in for oatmeal. In Québec, gruau is common, so a regional note may be needed.
Irregular verbs (prendre, boire, ouvrir) are included in the present-tense material. A native teacher should check whether the beginner pacing is right for these forms.
French café context here is the Mexico scene. A France or Québec variant with local dishes and currency is still needed.
Regular -ir verbs such as choisir are deferred from this beginner lesson; the source Spanish present-tense objective is mirrored through French -er and high-use irregular breakfast verbs instead.
